summary: This standards-track document defines a MIB module for managing ADSL, ADSL2, ADSL2+ and variant interface types. It provides objects network management systems can read and set to control and monitor these lines.

eli5.summary: DSL internet lines have settings and readouts. This is the list of the dials and gauges so a network operator can check the lines from far away.

questions: how do adsl2 profiles and templates work
subtitle: The SNMP management objects for monitoring and configuring ADSL, ADSL2 and ADSL2+ lines.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a standard way to configure, monitor and get alarms from ADSL2 and ADSL2+ lines. The older ADSL MIB in RFC 2662 covered only the first generation of ADSL.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4706 defines the ADSL2-LINE-MIB, a set of SNMP tables for line status, inventory, performance counters, reusable configuration profiles and templates, and threshold notifications. It sits under the MIB-2 transmission branch as number 238.
tldr.outcome: It does not obsolete RFC 2662. Lines with ifType adsl2plus(238) MUST be managed with this MIB, while ifType adsl(94) lines MUST use RFC 2662.

today: RFC 4706 is a Proposed Standard from November 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not replace RFC 2662, which remains the model for lines with ifType adsl(94).

sections.title: What the ADSL2 Line MIB Is
sections.content:
RFC 4706 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for the Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line family: ADSL, ADSL2, ADSL2+ and their variants. A MIB is a virtual information store that management software reads and writes, usually through SNMP. The module is written in SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).

The objects follow the ITU-T G.997.1 management model and the DSL Forum TR-90 framework for next-generation ADSL. Each object's REFERENCE clause points at the paragraph of G.997.1 it comes from. Managing VDSL2 lines is explicitly out of scope.
sections.eli5: Network gear keeps a big list of settings and readings about each DSL line. This document writes down exactly what is on that list, so every maker of gear uses the same names.

sections.title: Relationship to RFC 2662 and the Interfaces MIB
sections.content:
RFC 2662 already described ADSL lines per T1E1.413, G.992.1 and G.992.2. RFC 4706 does not obsolete it. It adds a more comprehensive model that covers ADSL2 and ADSL2+ per G.992.3, G.992.4 and G.992.5.

A separate interface type keeps the two models apart. IANA allocated ifType=adsl2plus(238), and also assigned transmission number 238 to the ADSL2-LINE-MIB module. Lines with ifType=adsl(94) MUST be managed with RFC 2662. ADSL, ADSL2 and ADSL2+ lines with adsl2plus(238) MUST be managed with this document.

The module plugs into the Interfaces MIB of RFC 2863. Channels can use ifType interleave(124), fast(125) or channel(70). The ifFixedLengthGroup MUST be supported, ifPhysAddress MUST be a zero-length octet string, and table entries indexed by ifIndex MUST be persistent.
sections.eli5: Think of an old rulebook and a new rulebook for two kinds of lines. A label on each line tells you which book to use, so nothing gets mixed up.

sections.title: Naming Conventions and Textual Conventions
sections.content:
An ADSL line has two ends. The ATU-C is the transceiver at the central office (the network operator) and the ATU-R is at the remote, subscriber end. XTU means either one. Upstream runs from ATU-R to ATU-C, downstream the other way.

The RFC defines a set of textual conventions that give typed names to values. Examples include Adsl2RaMode (manual, raInit or dynamicRa rate adaptation), Adsl2InitResult (from noFail(0) to otherCause(5)), Adsl2LineStatus (a BITS value reporting loss of frame, loss of signal, loss of power or an initialization failure) and Adsl2MaxBer (E^-3, E^-5 or E^-7).

Several conventions describe bit-level line settings: the downstream sub-carrier mask is a bitmap of up to 512 bits, the upstream one up to 64 bits, and the downstream PSD mask is up to 32 breakpoints of 3 octets each.
sections.eli5: Before listing the dials, the document agrees on names: which end of the wire is the phone company and which is your house, and what each light colour on a gauge means.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The module hangs under transmission 238 and splits into groups, each with its own tables.

  • Line configuration, maintenance and status: adsl2LineTable, which also holds commands such as forcing a power state or starting a Dual Ended Loop Test (DELT).
  • Channel status and sub-carrier status (mostly DELT results), and a unit inventory table read via the Embedded Operations Channel (EOC).
  • Performance groups: current, 15-minute history and 1-day history tables for the line, for initializations and for channels.
  • Profile groups: configuration templates and profiles, and alarm templates and profiles.
  • Notifications for status changes and threshold crossings.

An ADSL line consists of an ATU-C and an ATU-R joined by twisted pair. There are up to 4 channels, each carrying an independent information flow; channel 1 is always present and channels 2 to 4 are optional.
sections.eli5: The big list is sorted into folders: one for settings, one for current readings, one for history, one for saved presets, and one for alarms.

sections.title: Counters, Interval Buckets and Thresholds
sections.content:
Counters apply at three levels. On the whole line there are counters for full and short initializations and their failures. On each XTU there are LOS seconds, errored seconds (ES), severely errored seconds (SES), FEC seconds and unavailable seconds (UAS). On each bearer channel there are coding violations (CRC anomalies) and corrected blocks (FEC events).

Each counter has a current 15-minute bucket, 0 to 96 history buckets of 15 minutes, and a current plus 0 to 30 previous 1-day buckets. Implementations SHOULD support at least 16 fifteen-minute buckets, as G.997.1 says, and at least 1 previous-day bucket. Counters are not reset when an XTU reinitializes, only when the agent is reset or reinitialized.

If data for an interval is suspect, the agent MUST report the interval as invalid and MUST NOT generate notifications from it. The MIB also reports the actual monitoring time of an interval, so a partial interval or one stretched by a clock adjustment can still be declared valid.
sections.eli5: The line keeps a tally of its hiccups in 15-minute and one-day notebooks, and keeps the old pages for a while. If a page looks smudged, it says so instead of pretending it is right.

sections.title: Profiles and Templates
sections.content:
A managed node can serve hundreds or thousands of lines, and most are provisioned identically. So the MIB uses shared profiles. A line configuration profile covers the low layer: allowed ADSL modes and annexes, power spectrum, rate adaptation and SNR margins. A channel configuration profile covers the service layer, such as minimum and maximum data rates and impulse noise protection. A configuration template is a profile of profiles: one line profile plus one to four channel profiles.

Alarm thresholds work the same way with alarm profiles and alarm templates. A line is pointed at a template by name, for example silver, through adsl2LineCnfgTemplate and adsl2LineAlarmCnfgTemplate. Names are locally unique SnmpAdminString values.

Implementations MUST provide a default entry named DEFVAL for each profile and template type. A template MUST be unreferenced from all lines before it is deleted, and a profile from all templates. If a change is made to a profile in use, it MUST take effect immediately and MAY restart the units on the line.
sections.eli5: Instead of setting up each line by hand, you save a preset like "silver" and point lots of lines at it. Change the preset and every line using it changes too.

sections.title: Notifications and Bearer Channels
sections.content:
Generating coldStart and warmStart (per agent) and linkUp and linkDown (per interface) notifications is REQUIRED. The MIB adds its own notifications for status changes and for threshold crossings on full and short initialization failures, ES, SES, FEC seconds, LOS seconds, UAS, coding violations and corrected blocks. Each threshold has its own value, and a value of 0 disables that notification.

A threshold notification fires when the current 15-minute counter becomes equal to or exceeds the threshold, and only one SHOULD be sent per interval per interface. Because the counter resets every 15 minutes, a lasting condition can repeat as often as every 15 minutes. Setting a threshold to 1 gives a notification whenever the event occurs, at most once per interval. Other notifications SHOULD be rate-limited, and throttled ones are dropped rather than queued.

The number of bearer channels follows the template. When it rises, the agent creates rows in the channel status and current channel performance tables. When it falls, it destroys rows in those and in the channel history tables.
sections.eli5: Each alarm is a doorbell with a counter behind it. When the count of problems reaches the number you chose, it rings once, then waits for the next 15-minute round.

sections.title: Implementation Notes for ADSL Managers
sections.content:
A management application built for RFC 2662 needs changes to use this MIB with ADSL links. Templates can name 1 to 4 bearer channels, but ADSL links are limited to 2 channels at most. Impulse noise protection is given as minimum protection and maximum delay. The line profile has a mode-specific sub-table, and for ADSL links the manager SHOULD create a row there for the adsl mode.

Many profile and status parameters are irrelevant for some ADSL modes, so the RFC advises consulting G.997.1 for the scope of each parameter. Read-create objects and most read-write objects SHOULD be stored persistently, and the RFC lists them exhaustively. Rows in the sub-carrier status table are volatile and are lost if the agent reboots.
sections.eli5: If you used the old list before, a few things changed, so check which items still apply to your kind of line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access may be sensitive. SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can hurt network operations. The RFC lists the sensitive tables and what an attacker could do.

  • Changing adsl2LineCnfgTemplate could have a major effect on many lines at once.
  • adsl2LineCmndConfPmsf can alter power use and disrupt service.
  • adsl2LineCmndConfLdsf can trigger an unscheduled line test, and adsl2LineCmndAutomodeColdStart an unscheduled cold reset.
  • Template and profile changes can move several lines to unwanted settings or change the number of channels.

Deleting rows in the sub-carrier status table could erase test results too early.
sections.eli5: The dials that change things are like the controls on a power panel. Only trusted people should be allowed to touch them, or lots of lines could break at once.
